title: Conformity and Obedience
description: How groups and authority pressure individuals to comply

concepts.title: Asch's Line Studies
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1951, Solomon Asch ran experiments at Swarthmore College that became canonical demonstrations of normative social influence. Participants judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line. The task was easy — control subjects erred less than 1% of the time.

The twist: each participant sat with confederates instructed to give the same wrong answer on certain trials. About 75% of participants conformed at least once, and roughly a third of all critical responses matched the incorrect majority.

Crucially, the conformists were not stupid; many privately knew the right answer but went along to avoid social discomfort. Asch identified key moderators: a single ally giving the correct answer cut conformity dramatically, and conformity rose as group size grew up to about three or four — beyond that, additional confederates added little.

Asch's work distinguished going along publicly (compliance) from genuinely changing private belief (internalisation).

concepts.title: Milgram's Obedience Experiments
concepts.contentHtml:
Stanley Milgram, motivated by the Eichmann trial, asked in 1963 how far ordinary people would go in obeying authority. Participants at Yale were told they were testing learning. They were instructed to deliver electric shocks of increasing voltage to a 'learner' (a confederate) for each wrong answer, up to a labelled '450 volts — XXX'.

Milgram predicted only 1–3% would go to the maximum. In fact, about 65% of participants delivered the full 450-volt shock, despite hearing the learner scream, complain of a heart condition, and eventually fall silent. Most showed visible distress but continued when the experimenter calmly said 'the experiment requires that you continue'.

Key situational factors: physical proximity to the victim, proximity of authority, institutional setting, and the presence of disobedient peers all shifted obedience rates by tens of percentage points. Milgram concluded that destructive obedience reflects an agentic state in which people see themselves as instruments of a legitimate authority rather than as autonomous moral agents.

concepts.title: Informational vs Normative Influence
concepts.contentHtml:
Deutsch and Gerard (1955) drew a now-standard distinction between two reasons we conform.

Normative social influence: we go along to be liked, accepted, or to avoid social punishment. This typically produces public compliance without private belief change. Asch's line study is the textbook case — people knew the answer was wrong but did not want to look strange.

Informational social influence: when a situation is ambiguous, others' behaviour is evidence about reality. Sherif's autokinetic effect study (1936), in which a stationary point of light appears to move in a dark room, showed that group estimates converged and persisted privately — genuine internalisation.

Real situations usually mix both. A new employee copies their colleagues partly to fit in (normative) and partly because they are figuring out what good work looks like (informational). Ambiguity, importance, and group cohesion all amplify these pressures.

title: Group Dynamics and the Bystander Effect
description: How groups change individual behaviour, from helping to roles

concepts.title: The Bystander Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese in Queens — initially reported as having 38 unresponsive witnesses — prompted Bibb Latané and John Darley to ask why bystanders sometimes fail to help. (Later journalism showed the original news account was exaggerated, but the underlying phenomenon is real.)

In their 1968 'smoke-filled room' study, lone participants reported smoke seeping under a door 75% of the time within four minutes; in groups of three strangers, only 38% reported it, and many never did even as the room filled.

Latané and Darley proposed a five-step decision model: notice, interpret as emergency, assume responsibility, know how to help, and decide to act. Larger groups disrupt step three through diffusion of responsibility and step two through pluralistic ignorance — when each person looks at calm others and concludes nothing must be wrong.

concepts.title: The Stanford Prison Experiment
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1971, Philip Zimbardo recruited Stanford students, screened for psychological health, and randomly assigned them to play guards or prisoners in a mock prison in the basement of the psychology building. The study was planned for two weeks.

Within days, guards became increasingly authoritarian and humiliating; prisoners became withdrawn, anxious, and several broke down. Zimbardo, acting as superintendent, was himself drawn into the role. The study was halted after six days.

Zimbardo argued the results showed how readily ordinary people slip into cruel behaviour when situational forces — uniforms, role assignment, deindividuation, and authority — push them. Critics, especially after re-analyses by Le Texier and others, have argued that guards were coached toward harshness and that demand characteristics shaped the outcomes.

The lesson is now more nuanced: powerful situations matter, but so do the explicit norms and instructions of the people running them.

concepts.title: Groupthink and Group Polarisation
concepts.contentHtml:
Irving Janis (1972) coined groupthink to describe how cohesive groups under pressure can converge on poor decisions. Symptoms include illusions of invulnerability, suppression of dissent, self-censorship, and an illusion of unanimity. Janis's case studies included the Bay of Pigs invasion and the Challenger launch decision.

A separate but related phenomenon is group polarisation: after discussion, groups typically adopt positions more extreme than the average individual member started with. A group of mildly hawkish people becomes very hawkish; a group of mildly cautious people becomes very cautious.

Two mechanisms drive polarisation. Persuasive arguments: members hear new arguments supporting the leaning view. Social comparison: members shift to look slightly more like a 'good' group member than average, and the average drifts. Online echo chambers exhibit the same dynamics, helping explain the radicalising effect of homogeneous communities.

title: Attitudes and Persuasion
description: How attitudes form, change, and resist change

concepts.title: Cognitive Dissonance
concepts.contentHtml:
Leon Festinger's A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance (1957) proposed that holding inconsistent cognitions produces an unpleasant arousal that motivates change. We are not passive observers of our own attitudes — when actions and beliefs clash, beliefs often shift to follow behaviour.

The classic test came from Festinger and Carlsmith (1959). Participants performed a tedious task, then were paid either $1 or $20 to tell the next participant it was interesting. Surprisingly, those paid only $1 later reported finding the task more enjoyable than those paid $20. The $20 group could explain their lie by the money; the $1 group had no external justification, so they reduced dissonance by changing their attitude.

Dissonance reduction routes include changing the behaviour, changing the belief, adding consonant cognitions, or trivialising the conflict. The theory predicts effects in counter-attitudinal advocacy, post-decision regret, hazing and effort justification, and induced compliance.

concepts.title: The Elaboration Likelihood Model
concepts.contentHtml:
Richard Petty and John Cacioppo's Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM, 1986) proposes two routes through which persuasion operates.

The central route involves careful, effortful scrutiny of the message itself. When motivation and ability are high — the topic matters and there are no distractions — strong arguments produce durable, behaviour-relevant attitude change resistant to counter-arguments.

The peripheral route uses cues unrelated to the message's logical content: source attractiveness, message length as a proxy for substance, expert credentials, mood, or simple repetition. Peripheral persuasion is faster but produces weaker, less stable attitudes.

The same cue can act centrally or peripherally depending on involvement. A doctor's credentials are a peripheral cue if you are barely listening but become a relevant argument if you are weighing whether to trust their reasoning. Marketing, political campaigns, and health messaging routinely combine both — strong arguments for engaged audiences and peripheral cues for everyone else.

concepts.title: Compliance Techniques
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Cialdini's Influence (1984) catalogued robust techniques for getting people to say yes, grounded in basic principles of social psychology.

Foot-in-the-door (Freedman and Fraser, 1966): a small initial request makes a later large request more likely to succeed. Once people see themselves as the kind of person who agreed, consistency pressure does the rest.

Door-in-the-face: an outrageously large request is rejected, then a smaller target request feels reasonable by contrast and triggers reciprocal concession.

Low-balling: a buyer agrees to a deal, then the seller raises the cost. Many still go through with it because they feel committed.

Cialdini grouped influence under six principles: reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, and scarcity. Effective influence, ethical or otherwise, almost always rides on at least one of these.

title: Prejudice, Stereotyping, and Intergroup Conflict
description: How groups divide, categorise, and how contact can heal

concepts.title: Robbers Cave and Realistic Conflict Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1954 Muzafer Sherif ran a now-famous field study at Robbers Cave State Park in Oklahoma. Twenty-two boys, all white, middle-class, and pre-screened as well-adjusted, were split into two groups (the Rattlers and the Eagles) at separate camps.

Once each group had bonded, the experimenters introduced a tournament in which only one team could win prizes. Hostility escalated quickly — name-calling, raids, flag-burning, and food fights. Stereotyping each group held of the other became sharply negative within days.

The decisive intervention was not contact alone — bringing the groups together for meals only intensified hostility. What worked were superordinate goals: tasks that required both groups to cooperate, like fixing the camp water supply or pulling a stuck truck. Cooperation toward shared ends gradually dissolved the rivalry.

Sherif's conclusion — realistic conflict theory — is that competition over scarce resources generates prejudice; cooperation toward shared goals reduces it.

concepts.title: Social Identity Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Henri Tajfel and John Turner showed in the 1970s that intergroup bias does not even require resource conflict. In the minimal group paradigm, participants assigned to groups by trivial criteria — preference for Klee or Kandinsky paintings, or even a coin toss — still allocated more rewards to in-group members than out-group members, even at cost to absolute in-group payoffs.

Tajfel's Social Identity Theory argues that part of our self-concept derives from group memberships. To maintain positive self-esteem, we are motivated to see our groups as positively distinct from others. This produces in-group favouritism, out-group derogation, and, when groups are perceived as threatening, hostility.

Three processes: social categorisation (sorting people into us and them), social identification (adopting the identity), and social comparison (comparing in-group with out-group). The theory helps explain phenomena from sports rivalries to nationalism to corporate tribalism, and the way trivial categories can become weighty under threat.

concepts.title: Stereotypes, Implicit Bias, and Contact
concepts.contentHtml:
Stereotypes are cognitive shortcuts: generalisations about social groups that simplify a complex social world but distort it systematically. They become prejudice when they carry negative affect and discrimination when they shape behaviour.

Patricia Devine (1989) distinguished automatic activation of cultural stereotypes from controlled responses. Even people who consciously reject a stereotype may have it activated automatically by cues. The Implicit Association Test (Greenwald et al. 1998) measures such automatic associations, though its predictive validity for individual behaviour and the stability of scores have been challenged in recent years — important caveats from the replication crisis.

Gordon Allport's contact hypothesis (1954) proposed that prejudice declines when groups meet under four conditions: equal status, common goals, intergroup cooperation, and institutional support. Decades of meta-analysis (Pettigrew and Tropp) confirm contact reduces prejudice on average, though the optimal-conditions caveats matter.

title: Social Cognition and the Replication Crisis
description: How we read others, the errors we make, and what survived re-examination

concepts.title: The Fundamental Attribution Error
concepts.contentHtml:
Lee Ross (1977) named the fundamental attribution error (FAE): our tendency to over-attribute others' behaviour to stable dispositions and under-attribute it to situations.

In Jones and Harris (1967), participants read essays for or against Castro and were told the writer had been assigned the position. Even knowing this, observers inferred the writer privately held the position they had been forced to defend.

The FAE shows up in everyday life: someone who cuts you off in traffic is a jerk; when you do the same, you were running late. It is moderated by culture — work by Joan Miller and others suggests it is weaker in many East Asian samples, who more readily invoke situational explanations.

A related bias is the actor–observer asymmetry: we explain our own behaviour situationally and others' dispositionally — partly because we have richer access to our own situational pressures.

concepts.title: Heuristics and Self-Serving Biases
concepts.contentHtml:
Tversky and Kahneman's heuristics-and-biases programme reshaped social cognition. Among many findings:

Availability heuristic: we judge frequency by ease of recall. Vivid news coverage of plane crashes makes flying feel more dangerous than it is.

Representativeness heuristic: we judge probability by similarity to a stereotype, often ignoring base rates — the 'Linda problem' is a famous demonstration.

Anchoring: arbitrary starting numbers bias subsequent estimates.

People also display systematic motivated biases. The self-serving bias attributes our successes to ability and our failures to circumstance. The false consensus effect overestimates how many others share our views and behaviour. The confirmation bias selectively seeks and weights information that supports existing beliefs.

These biases are normal cognitive operating modes, not pathology — but social psychology's job is to map them, predict where they distort, and design environments that correct rather than amplify them.

concepts.title: The Replication Crisis and What Survived
concepts.contentHtml:
From around 2011, social psychology entered a period of public reckoning. Daniel Kahneman wrote an open letter warning of a 'train wreck'. The Open Science Collaboration's 2015 replication of 100 psychology studies reproduced significant effects in only about 36% of cases, with social-psychology effects faring worse than cognitive ones.

Several headline findings shrank or vanished on reanalysis: ego depletion, social priming studies (elderly-words slowing walking), and the 'power posing' physiology effects all proved fragile. The Stanford Prison Experiment was reframed by archival research as more directed and less spontaneous than the original narrative suggested.

What survived has been clarified by larger, pre-registered, multi-site replications: Asch-style conformity, the bystander effect (with smaller estimated size), Milgram-style obedience patterns, dissonance after counter-attitudinal advocacy, and contact-hypothesis benefits. The lesson is methodological humility: prefer pre-registered, well-powered, multi-lab evidence; treat single dramatic studies as hypotheses, not conclusions.
